methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective observational cohort of 154 adult Ph+ B-ALL patients across 2001–2019 (Section 2.1). The design is appropriate for descriptive outcomes but weak for causal claims about asparaginase and CR1 alloSCT omission since cohort era is strongly confounded with changes in supportive care, TKI practice patterns, and donor availability; the authors acknowledge selection bias but mitigate it only by era-stratification and multivariable adjustment, with no propensity-score or landmark analyses to address immortal-time bias beyond modeling alloSCT as a time-varying covariate (Section 3.2). The transplanted and non-transplanted groups differ significantly by age (46 vs 55 years, p<0.001; Section 3) yet no formal matching is performed. Statistical methods are generally correct — Kaplan–Meier, log-rank, Cox with a time-varying alloSCT covariate, and reporting of HRs with 95% CIs — but no power calculation is given, no multiplicity correction is applied across the many univariable comparisons in Table 2, no handling of missing MRD data is described, and the final 2016–2019 non-alloSCT subgroup (n=23) is too small to support strong conclusions about the primary clinical message.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study is an individual retrospective cohort analysis of consecutively treated adult Ph+ B-ALL patients at a single academic centre, which maps to Oxford CEBM level 2b. The clinical question — whether routine CR1 alloSCT can be safely omitted when MRD-guided decision-making is applied in adults receiving pediatric-inspired chemotherapy plus imatinib — is highly relevant and directly addresses a controversy explicitly flagged in current EBMT, NCCN, and ASTCT guidance (Section 1). Endpoints are patient-relevant (OS, RFS) with mature follow-up (median 41.1 months, maximum ~228 months), and the findings align with and extend prior work by Ravandi (2013) and Short (2016), supporting a plausible path to influence practice patterns and guideline language in centres still mandating CR1 alloSCT. The relevance is moderated by the retrospective single-centre design and by the fact that the field is already moving toward blinatumomab-based frontline regimens (D-ALBA, GIMEMA ALL2820).

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE applies as this is a retrospective observational cohort. The manuscript reports the setting, period, eligibility, exclusions (three patients with non-protocol initial therapy), outcome definitions (BCR::ABL1 molecular response thresholds, relapse criteria, OS/RFS start times in Section 2.2), and statistical methods including software version, which covers many STROBE items. However, there is no participant flow diagram, no explicit handling of missing data, no clear description of how the covariates in the multivariable model were selected, no sensitivity analyses, and no quantification of potential confounder effects or discussion of generalizability beyond a brief limitations paragraph. Data availability is not addressed in the retained text and no repository, code, or protocol link is provided; raw per-patient data and analytic code are not referenced, consistent with a score of 2.

novelty_literature.justification: The central message — that MRD-guided omission of CR1 alloSCT is feasible in adult Ph+ B-ALL on TKI-containing regimens — is explicitly incremental, and the manuscript itself cites multiple directly comparable prior reports (Ravandi 2013 [20], Short 2016 [23], Chalandon 2015 [21], Jabbour 2018 [24], Badar 2023 [22]) that have already advanced the same thesis, several with newer-generation TKIs and larger series. The novelty lies in longitudinal institutional data showing iterative protocol change (asparaginase omission in 2009, alloSCT de-escalation from the early 2010s) using the pediatric-inspired PM-DFCI backbone with imatinib, which is a population/protocol-specific extension rather than a conceptual or methodological innovation. The field is already pivoting toward blinatumomab- and ponatinib-based chemotherapy-sparing approaches (D-ALBA, GIMEMA ALL2820), further limiting the originality of an imatinib-era retrospective. No new assay, mechanism, or framework is introduced.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and logically organized: the introduction frames guideline tension (EBMT vs NCCN vs ASTCT) and the two protocol changes under study, the methods section is concise, and the results are reported with HRs, 95% CIs, and p-values that are consistent between text and the described tables. The discussion sensibly contextualizes findings against UKALLXII, UKALL14, Ravandi, Short, Jabbour, D-ALBA, and GIMEMA ALL2820 and is appropriately cautious about the ponatinib meta-analysis. Minor issues include an occasional abstract-style redundancy at the top of the Abstract, a stray typographical artifact ('[REDACTED]–2019'), small numerical inconsistency between the 2001–2009 cohort OS/RFS quoted in Section 3.1 (50.0/39.4 split) and the Discussion (44.4% / 42.5% aggregate), and a '95 CI' typo. Captions are not available for direct assessment but figures are called out meaningfully in the text.

key_strengths: Addresses a clinically important and guideline-contested question (routine CR1 alloSCT vs MRD-guided omission) in adult Ph+ B-ALL
Long accrual window (2001–2019) with mature follow-up and iterative within-institution protocol changes that enable era-stratified comparison
Appropriate use of Cox models with alloSCT as a time-varying covariate, mitigating classical immortal-time bias
Clear positioning against directly relevant literature including UKALLXII, UKALL14, Ravandi 2013, Short 2016, D-ALBA, and GIMEMA ALL2820
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design with strong confounding between calendar era, supportive care, and the two interventions of interest; no propensity-score or matched analyses
Key subgroup driving the headline (2016–2019 non-alloSCT) is only 23 patients, with wide CIs (4-year OS 87.0%, 64.8–95.6%)
No power calculation, no multiplicity correction across the many univariate comparisons in Table 2, and no description of missing MRD data handling
Novelty is incremental — same conclusion already advanced by multiple cited groups with newer TKIs and larger series
STROBE adherence is partial (no flow diagram, limited missing-data and confounder-selection reporting) and data/code availability is not stated
Minor numerical inconsistencies between results text and discussion (e.g., 2001–2009 OS/RFS figures) and a stray '[REDACTED]' artifact
chief_reviewer.rationale: Tier 3 (BJC/EJC/BMC Cancer range) is the highest plausible fit: the clinical question is important and the analysis is competent, but the design is a single-centre retrospective imatinib-era series whose main message is incremental to already-published multicentre data, which precludes Tier 1 or Tier 2. Major revisions are warranted to strengthen confounding control (e.g., landmark/propensity analyses), add STROBE-style reporting, and temper the practice-changing framing given the small decisive subgroup.
